title: How Your Phone Finds You Without Talking to Space | How It Works #7
simplified: Simplified model: drawn in 2D (circles instead of spheres), satellites and distances not to scale, signal travel exaggerated in slow motion; the 'clock error cancels' step is shown as rings snapping to one point.

hook_candidates.text: Your phone never answers these satellites. So how does it find you?
This blue dot knows where you are. Nobody told it.
Watch this circle. It has to shrink to your exact street.
You opened maps. Twenty thousand kilometres up, nothing heard you.
A millionth of a second wrong, and you're three hundred metres lost.

sources: Receive-only: GPS 'was to be a passive system, which ruled out any transmissions from the users'. Penn State GEOG 862, NAVSTAR GPS, https://courses.ems.psu.edu/geog862/node/1768

Satellites broadcast time from atomic clocks; receiver uses travel time: 'Each satellite transmits its position and time at regular intervals'; 'The receiver is able to determine its position by calculating how long it took for the signals to reach it'; satellites 'each equipped with redundant atomic clocks'. NASA SCaN, What is GPS?, https://www.nasa.gov/general/what-is-gps/
Distance from delay: 'Distance = Speed of Light * Time Difference'. Penn State, Nature of Geographic Information, 17. Satellite Ranging, https://courses.ems.psu.edu/natureofgeoinfo/web/node/1796
One microsecond error = about 300 m: speed of light 299,792,458 m/s (SI definition) x 0.000001 s = 299.8 m. On screen as 300 M (about 1,000 FT).

Receiver clocks are cheap: GPS receivers have quartz clocks 'less stable than the atomic clocks used in NAVSTAR satellites'; 'Receiver clock error can be eliminated, however, by comparing times of arrival of signals from two satellites'. Penn State, 19. User Equivalent Range Errors, https://courses.ems.psu.edu/natureofgeoinfo/web/node/1798

More satellites: 'Four ranges are needed for a three-dimensional fix'; 'a minimum of four satellites is always in view everywhere on Earth'. Penn State, 17. Satellite Ranging (above). Four satellites drawn on screen.
Accuracy 'a few metres': GPS 'can pinpoint a three dimensional position to meter-level accuracy'. NASA SCaN (above). Orbit 'about 20,200 kilometers' (NASA, above), not spoken.
